stemMd:
Of the four instruments carried aloft by the research balloon, only one returned usable ______ whose readings, taken every thirty seconds during the ascent, were later used to chart the temperature of the upper atmosphere.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanationMd:
Three of these choices treat what follows the blank as a second sentence, so test that first: does *the thermometer, whose readings, taken every thirty seconds during the ascent, were later used to chart the temperature of the upper atmosphere* have a main verb?

It looks as though it does, because it contains *were later used*. But look at what *were* agrees with. It is plural, so it cannot belong to *the thermometer*; it belongs to *readings*, inside the relative clause that begins with *whose*. Strip that clause out and what is left is just *the thermometer*, a noun phrase with no verb of its own. It is not an independent clause.

So the words after the blank cannot follow a semicolon or a period, and cannot be joined by *and* as a second clause. What they do is name the "one" instrument that the first clause mentions, and a colon after a complete clause is exactly the mark that introduces such an identification. The answer is **data: the thermometer,**.

Check by reading the key as "only one returned usable data, and that one was the thermometer". The colon does the work of *and that one was*.

distractorRationale.b: A semicolon must have an independent clause on each side. What follows it here is 'the thermometer' plus a relative clause; the verb 'were later used' belongs to 'readings' inside that clause, so the thermometer itself has no verb and the second half is a fragment.
distractorRationale.c: This starts a new sentence with 'The thermometer', but that sentence never gives the thermometer a verb: 'were later used' belongs to 'readings' within the 'whose' clause. The result is a sentence fragment, the same flaw as the semicolon, disguised by the length of the relative clause.
distractorRationale.d: Read as ', and' joining a second clause, the second part has no main verb for 'the thermometer', so it is a fragment. Read instead as adding 'the thermometer' as a second thing the instrument returned, it makes no sense, since the thermometer is the one instrument rather than something that instrument sent back, and a comma should not split a two-part object in any case.

accessibilityText: A sentence saying that of the four instruments carried by a research balloon, only one returned usable data, followed by a blank and then a relative clause beginning 'whose readings, taken every thirty seconds during the ascent, were later used to chart the temperature of the upper atmosphere.' Each choice contains the word data and the words the thermometer followed by a comma, with different punctuation between them: a colon; a semicolon; a period with The capitalized; and a comma followed by the word and.

provenance.notes: Original item. The balloon flight and its instruments are invented; no source text was adapted.

independentSolve.workingNotes: After the blank, 'the thermometer, whose readings ... were later used ...' has no main verb of its own: 'were used' belongs to the relative clause. So it can only be an appositive naming the 'one' instrument, and a colon introduces that correctly. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave7-sat-rw-run1) reached the same answer: What follows the blank, 'the thermometer, whose readings... were later used...', is a noun phrase with a relative clause and no main verb. So it cannot stand as its own clause after a semicolon (B) or a period (C). A colon correctly introduces it as the identification of 'only one'.]

review.notes: Author's own solve and uniqueness check: After the blank, 'the thermometer' is followed only by a non-restrictive 'whose' clause whose verb 'were' is plural and so agrees with 'readings', not 'thermometer'. The material after the blank is therefore a noun phrase, not an independent clause, so semicolon, period and ', and' all produce a fragment; the colon correctly introduces the identity of 'only one'. A plain comma and a dash were deliberately kept out of the choice set because an appositive after a comma or a dash could also be defended. Re-solved from the stem alone: same answer. Unique. STRETCH: harder than a typical hard boundaries item because the fragment masquerades as a full clause: it contains a finite verb and a nested interruption, so the candidate must use agreement (plural 'were' cannot take the singular 'thermometer') to prove that the verb is trapped inside the relative clause. Three of the four choices fail for that single hidden reason, so elimination by ear does not work. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
